analysis.title: US Daily: September Payrolls Preview
key_insights: GS estimates September nonfarm payrolls rose 80k, slightly below consensus of +88k and above the three-month average of +71k. Private payrolls are estimated at +75k vs consensus +80k.

Layoffs argue for a stronger report: initial jobless claims averaged 204k in the September payroll month, in line with August. The JOLTS layoff rate fell 0.1pp to 1.0% in August. Challenger announced layoffs fell 2k to 52k in September (SA by GS).
Alternative employment data picked up: the indicators GS tracks averaged +77k in September vs +31k in August, slightly below the consensus estimate.
A late Labor Day (September 7th) argues for a weaker report. In past Septembers with a Labor Day that late, payroll growth has generally underperformed the recent trend.

August job growth was overstated. Rebounds in local government educational services and leisure and hospitality contributed a combined 104k, likely a normalization after similar declines over the prior two months. GS does not expect a repeat. Seasonal adjustment is difficult for these series, which adds volatility.

Job openings were roughly unchanged in August across JOLTS, Indeed and LinkUp, and the Indeed and LinkUp measures were stable in September. The Conference Board labor differential fell 2.5pt to +1.7 in September.

Employment components of GS's manufacturing (+1.0pt to 53.2) and services (+1.4pt to 51.4) survey trackers rose in September. GS says survey data has been less useful post-pandemic and has little bearing on the payrolls forecast.

GS estimates average hourly earnings rose 0.2% m/m in September, below consensus of 0.3%, reflecting negative calendar effects. The GS wage tracker is up 3.1% q/q annualized and 3.5% y/y in Q3 (preliminary).
GS estimates the unemployment rate edged down to 4.0% (rounded) from 4.1% in August, reflecting the decline in continuing claims. Its previous forecast was in line with consensus at 4.1%.

The GS slack tracker, which combines ten measures of labor market slack in unemployment-rate-equivalent units, has declined in recent months but stands at 4.6%. GS reads this as a labor market somewhat softer than the unemployment rate alone implies.

risk_factors: A late Labor Day (September 7th) has historically coincided with September payrolls underperforming trend.
August strength in local education and leisure and hospitality payrolls (a combined 104k) may not repeat and may reverse.
Seasonal adjustment difficulty in local education and leisure and hospitality payrolls raises the volatility of monthly readings.
Survey-based employment signals have been less reliable post-pandemic.
charts_described: Exhibit 1 shows alternative measures of employment growth implied for September 2026, with Homebase at 55k, Census Business Pulse at 80k, consensus at 88k and ADP at 95k (ADP includes GS's assumed 5k government payroll increase).
Exhibit 2 plots September payroll growth vs the prior 3-month average in years with a September 7th Labor Day (1992, 1998, 2009, 2015, 2020), with one label at -438k.
Exhibit 4 plots the 4-week moving average of continuing claims and short-term unemployment (0-26 weeks) from January 2024 to September 2026.

tension_points.bull_case: Layoffs remain low (claims averaging 204k, JOLTS layoff rate 1.0%, Challenger layoffs 52k) and alternative data averaged +77k vs +31k in August.
tension_points.bear_case: A late Labor Day has historically coincided with September payroll underperformance, and August was boosted by a combined 104k from local education and leisure and hospitality that GS does not expect to repeat.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A payroll print well above the +88k consensus would show the late Labor Day and August reversal effects did not bind.

theme_stances.key_argument: September payroll growth tends to underperform trend when Labor Day falls late, and August was boosted by outsized increases GS does not expect to repeat.
theme_stances.evidence: payroll growth has generally underperformed the recent trend
